shipped_rows.title_o: Spending Money on Others Promotes Happiness

blind_target.authors: Aknin, L. B., Barrington-Leigh, C. P., Dunn, E. W., Helliwell, J. F., Burns, J., Biswas-Diener, R., . . . Norton, M. I.
blind_target.title: Prosocial spending and well-being: Cross-cultural evidence for a psychological universal.
blind_target.evidence_quote: The first experiment investigated the immediate emotional rewards of prosocial (vs. personal) spending by providing participants the opportunity to spend a small monetary windfall on edible treats for themselves or an unknown sick child at a local children’s hospital (see Aknin et al., 2013, Study 3). Afterward, participants reported their current well-being. The second experiment used a recollection procedure (as in Aknin et al., 2013, Studies 2a-b) in which participants were randomly assigned to reflect upon a previous purchase made for themselves or others before reporting their well-being.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Taken together, these studies support the hypothesis that spending money on others does promote happiness, but demonstrate that the magnitude of the effect depends on several methodological features.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The authors give an overall positive verdict across the three studies, so rule 1 determines successful. Experiment 2 failed and Experiments 1 and 3 supported the prediction; the explicit whole-project conclusion outweighs those differing individual results. Smaller effects do not alone imply mixed.

luna_triage.reason: The source explicitly identifies both experiments as tests of Aknin et al. (2013), Study 3 and Studies 2a–b, and states the predicted prosocial-versus-personal spending happiness comparison. The supplied row 468 is Dunn, Aknin, and Norton (2008), a separate original paper; the source distinguishes it as the original paradigm and says the Aknin goody-bag paradigm was adopted instead.
